html:
The Battle of Tours, also called Poitiers, was fought in October 732 between a Frankish army under Charles Martel and an Umayyad force from al-Andalus, somewhere between the French towns of Tours and Poitiers.

The Muslim army was led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, governor of al-Andalus. After the conquest of Spain, it had held Narbonne since 719 and raided deep into Gaul. The raid of 732 was a large one, aimed at the rich shrine of Saint Martin at Tours. The Franks, mostly foot soldiers, held a defensive position and the raiders failed to break them. Abd al-Rahman was killed, and the Muslim army withdrew.

Charles was mayor of the palace, the real ruler of the Franks. The victory raised his name, and his son Pepin and grandson Charlemagne built the Carolingian Empire on that power. Later writers, from Gibbon to the nineteenth century, made the battle the moment Europe was saved. Most historians now see it as one clash in a long series of raids, not the end of an invasion. Charles fought for Aquitaine and Provence for years afterward. The earlier Battle of Toulouse had gone the other way.
